Smart contracts are a unique form of computer code, in that once deployed to an immutable blockchain they are difficult to update. In the case of Cardano, the smart contract's code is also used to derive the address used to interact with it. Changing the code therefore results in a new address, which could make it difficult for applications interacting with the smart contract, as assets held in UTxOs of the original address may be unavailable from the new smart contract iteration and corresponding address.

For this reason any bugs that could pose a risk to the security of a smart contract need to be detected and addressed prior to deployment. Code audits allow specialised teams to detect potential bugs or vulnerabilities in smart contracts that may not have been identified by the original development team. As the marketplace smart contracts used in this project have been open sourced, anyone who wishes to use them as part of their own application will benefit from knowing that they have been audited for potential security risks.

The smart contracts audit was completed by Anastasia Labs.
They identified 9 areas in the code that needed review, with varying severity ratings. There were 1 Major, 3 Minor and 5 Informational findings. Issues that required action were corrected and Anastasia Labs reviewed the updates to confirm the issues identified were resolved in the updated code.
To confirm the completion of this milestone, the final audit report is now available on the project's open source GitHub repo, at https://github.com/empowa-io/ecosystem-marketplace/blob/main/audit/anastasia-labs-audit-report.pdf
If the reviewers have any questions about the completeness of this audit, then please feel free to contact me for a follow up discussion.

When developing application code, many programmers like to test that their code is resulting in the expected outputs before deploying it and getting support requests from users due to problems they experience. In order to do so, a common approach is to use testing frameworks that allow execution of the code to be scripted (a programmatic way of providing inputs to the application code) so that different input variations can be tested easier than doing so manually. By simplifying the execution of tests using different inputs, various scenarios can be tested to see how the application code responds. This might include deliberately supplying incorrect inputs, to ensure that the code can properly deal with unusual interactions and not cause data to be impacted unexpectedly when doing so. This is sometimes referred to as testing for both the "happy path" and the "sad path", as testing for unexpected or invalid user interactions is often more important than testing for when a user interacts with the application in the expected way.

The code for this project has been split into 2 repositories, as follows:
Smart Contracts - https://github.com/Vaka-Consulting/ecosystem-marketplace-contracts
Off-chain Application - https://github.com/Vaka-Consulting/ecosystem-marketplace-app

These repositories provide documentation on how to configure and deploy an instance of the ecosystem marketplace. An example instance is able to be deployed using the Docker compose files provided, although developers are encouraged to tailor their instance to suit their infrastructure requirements/platform. A demo instance (running on PreProd) has also been deployed to https://marketplace-app.dev.vakaconsulting.io/ for milestone reviewers to assess.

Finally, a video which shows what has been delivered as well as a deployment walkthrough is available at https://drive.google.com/file/d/1OxaLQOyhyydEomsGhWD5uUYvrRJXMAHl/view 

The close-out report (which includes a link to the close-out video) for this project is available https://drive.google.com/file/d/10R10wbBXFNgbc0B-8vIJSwk23XdeYJDD
